body.objective: Students will be able to scan for key, metre and road map.
body.iCan: I can scan for key, metre and road map.
successCriteria: I can scan a piece for key, metre, tempo and road map before playing
I can recognize rhythmic and melodic patterns
I can recover quickly from mistakes while sight-reading
body.hook: Professional session musicians are often handed music minutes before recording and play it nearly perfectly on the first take. They're not magic readers; they scan the page in a systematic way and recognize patterns instead of reading note by note.

vocabulary.definition: A quick, systematic look through music before playing.
The order of sections, repeats, endings and jumps.
Go back to the sign, then jump to the coda at the coda sign.
Seeing groups of notes (scales, arpeggios, rhythms) as whole units.
Looking at the next notes while playing the current ones.
Getting back in after a mistake without stopping.

study.title: Read Like a Pro
study.question: How do advanced musicians sight-read complex music accurately?
study.passage:
Part 1, The 60-second scan (10 minutes): Use this order: (1) Key signature and any key changes; (2) Time signature and changes; (3) Tempo and style markings; (4) Road map: trace repeats, first and second endings, D.S. (dal segno, from the sign 𝄋), D.C. (da capo, from the beginning), al Coda (jump to the coda ⊕), Fine; (5) Hardest rhythms: count them silently; (6) Accidentals and range extremes; (7) Dynamics and articulations.
Part 2, Patterns (10 minutes): Look at a page and circle scales, arpeggios and repeated rhythms. Name them ("B-flat arpeggio," "same rhythm as bar 3").
Part 3, Reading ahead (10 minutes): Play a simple exercise while the teacher covers the bar you are playing with a card, forcing your eyes forward.
Part 4, Recovery (5 minutes): Play with a recording; when you make a mistake, don't stop. Find the next downbeat or the next phrase.
Part 5, Test (15 minutes): Sight-read two new pieces: one band excerpt with a D.S. al Coda, and one solo excerpt with mixed metre. Self-rate rhythm, notes, road map and recovery.
study.source: Original sight-reading workshop written for this lesson.

study.product: Sight-read an unseen piece with a complex road map after a 60-second scan, then submit your annotated scan and a self-rating.

examples.title: Road map
examples.problem: Trace: A, B (with 𝄋 at start of B), C, "D.S. al Coda," coda sign at end of B, Coda.
examples.answer: A, B, C, back to B, jump at the coda sign to the Coda
examples.explore: Where would Fine end a D.C. al Fine?

examples.title: Pattern
examples.problem: You see B♭, D, F, B♭ ascending. What is it?
examples.explore: Why read it as one unit?

examples.title: Key change
examples.problem: Halfway through, the key signature changes to three flats. What do you do in the scan?
examples.answer: Circle it and note the new key (E-flat major or C minor)

examples.title: Recovery
examples.problem: You miss a note in bar 14. What's your plan?
examples.answer: Keep counting, rejoin at bar 15 or the next phrase

practice.a: A quick look through music before playing.
Da capo, go back to the beginning.
Dal segno, go back to the sign.
A closing section you jump to.

practice.q: What should you check first in a scan?

practice.a: Seeing groups of notes as whole units.
To prepare for the next notes before you reach them.

practice.q: What does D.S. al Coda tell you to do?
practice.a: Go back to the sign, then jump to the coda at the coda sign.

practice.q: Why count the hardest rhythms before playing?
practice.a: To avoid rhythm errors when you reach them.
Rejoining after a mistake without stopping.

practice.q: Why is recovery more important than perfection?
practice.a: In ensembles the music keeps going; stopping causes more errors.

practice.q: How can pattern recognition help with fast passages?
practice.a: You read groups like scales or arpeggios instead of each note.

practice.q: How should you handle a key change you missed in the scan?
practice.a: Keep going, listen and adjust; mark it next time.

practice.q: What does an advanced sight-reader do with dynamics on a first read?
practice.a: Plays them, because they are part of the music, not extras.

misconceptions: Reading one note at a time
Ignoring dynamics and articulations on a first read
exitTicket: List the first four steps of the scan.

test.title: Practice test: Scan for key, metre and road map

items.q: D.C. means
options: A) go back to the beginning
items.answer: A) go back to the beginning

items.q: D.S. means
options: D) go back to the sign
items.answer: D) go back to the sign

items.q: A coda is
options: D) a closing section you jump to
items.answer: D) a closing section you jump to

items.q: Fine means
items.answer: B) the end

items.q: The first step of a sight-reading scan is
items.answer: B) key signature

items.q: Seeing B♭-D-F-B♭ as one arpeggio is
items.answer: C) pattern recognition

items.q: D.S. al Coda tells you to
options: A) go to the beginning and end at Fine
D) go to the sign, then jump to the coda
items.answer: D) go to the sign, then jump to the coda

items.q: Reading ahead means
options: D) looking at upcoming notes while playing
items.answer: D) looking at upcoming notes while playing

items.q: Why count the hardest rhythms before playing?
options: D) To avoid errors when you reach them
items.answer: D) To avoid errors when you reach them

items.q: When you make a mistake sight-reading in a band, you should
items.answer: B) keep going and rejoin

items.q: Pattern recognition helps most with
options: B) fast scalar and arpeggio passages
items.answer: B) fast scalar and arpeggio passages

items.q: On a first read, dynamics should be
options: C) played as part of the music
items.answer: C) played as part of the music

items.q: What does D.C. al Fine mean?
items.answer: Go back to the beginning and end at Fine.

items.q: What is a coda?
items.answer: A closing section reached by a jump.

items.q: List the steps of a 60-second scan.
items.answer: Key, metre, tempo/style, road map, hard rhythms, accidentals/range, dynamics/articulations.

items.q: Explain pattern recognition with an example.
items.answer: Reading a scale or arpeggio as one unit.

items.q: Why is reading ahead important?
items.answer: It prepares you for the next notes.

items.q: Trace a D.S. al Coda road map in your own words.
items.answer: Go back to the sign, play to the coda sign, jump to the coda.

items.q: Explain why recovery is a key sight-reading skill.
items.answer: The ensemble keeps going, so rejoining matters more than one wrong note.

items.q: Describe how you would improve your sight-reading over a month.
items.answer: Answers vary; daily new reading, scanning, patterns.
